# Natural Swing-Up of an Underpowered Double Pendulum
## I Introduction
Swinging up a robot whose motors cannot even hold its arm horizontal is a matter of timing, not of force. The direct-drive motors of the planar two-link robot of Fig. 1 deliver only 1.1 Nm, about 6 % of the gravity torque in the first joint with the arm held horizontally. With full torque in both joints, link 2 tilts by 16.3^∘ and link 1 stays hanging, because the reaction of the elbow torque cancels the shoulder torque (Fig. 1b).
Neither a joint PD controller nor a controller that tracks a direct path to the upright pose (Fig. 5a) can get there; the robot has to collect the energy over many swings. A single pendulum is swung up by energy control, which puts it on the homoclinic orbit that ends upright [1]. The double pendulum is chaotic [2], so energy control alone most likely ends in chaotic motion, and energy-based swing-ups of double pendulums pass through intermediate equilibria [3, 4].
We instead guide the swing-up along the NNMs of the robot [5, 6, 7], families of periodic orbits of the free dynamics, one per energy. On one mode the robot behaves much like a single pendulum: there is no chaos, and the modes connect the hanging equilibrium to a homoclinic orbit at the upright one [8]. Pumping energy along a mode thus carries the robot from rest to almost upright, where a short precomputed trajectory catches it in a handstand.
## III Power-Based Input Split and CLF Allocation
A swing-up along a mode poses two problems that we want to decouple. Mode stabilization keeps the state on the mode, wherever in the family of orbits the robot currently is. Pumping injects energy, so that the robot climbs from orbit to orbit, and stops at the energy goal. On a non-strict mode the two interfere, and both must share the same bounded torque.

## Abstract

This paper presents a unified treatment of the motion control of underactuated two-link manipulators, including acrobots and pendubots. The motion space is divided into two areas: swing-up and attractive; and control laws are designed for each. First, a control law based on a weak-control Lyapunov function (WCLF) is employed to increase the energy of and control the posture of the actuated link in the swing-up area. Next, one parameter of the WCLF is chosen to be a nonlinear function of the state to avoid singularities. Then, another parameter of the control law is adjusted based on the state to improve the control performance. Finally, an optimal control law is designed for the attractive area. Stability is guaranteed in the swing-up area by the use of a WCLF based on LaSalle's invariance principle. Moreover, the global stability of the control system is guaranteed by integrating the WCLF and a nonsmooth Lyapunov function.

# Weak Robots Learn to Swing Up Like a Playground Swing

⚡This could let cheap robots do heavy lifting without expensive motors.

Deep Dive

Weak motors don’t have to fight a robot’s natural dynamics—they can ride them. A direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6% of its shoulder gravity torque, was swung up along its nonlinear normal modes: two-dimensional invariant manifolds made of periodic orbits.

On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque. The approach splits input torque into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input—the only component that changes the energy.

The allocation becomes a linear program in two variables: maximize pumping subject to torque limits and one control-Lyapunov constraint. That constraint uses the model-based rate of the error, so no stabilizing feedback gain is needed. Hardware experiments show swing-ups along both modes and compare the allocation with summing-and-clipping and with prioritized stabilization.

Key Points

- A two-jointed robot with motors only 6% as strong as needed learned to swing upright by pumping energy like a pendulum.
- This could lead to cheaper, lighter robots that use less power for tasks like lifting or moving.
- The method works on real hardware but is specific to certain robot designs and requires precise timing.

### Why It Matters

Cheaper, efficient robots could soon assist in homes and factories, saving money and energy.

*   UCLA Samueli and University of Michigan roboticists have shown that elastic rods can be bent and twisted to repeatedly snap between shapes.

Roboticists at the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering and the University of Michigan have shown that elastic rods can be bent and twisted to repeatedly snap between shapes, releasing built-up energy that enables small robots to hop, flip and swim.

The study, [published in Science Advances,](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aeh2779) could offer a promising new approach to movement for robots constrained by size, weight and power output. The snapping mechanism could also help robots move across uneven terrain, on land and in water.

###### Abstract

Robots with weak motors must ride their natural dynamics rather than fight them. We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6 % of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits. On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque. We split the input torque into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy. The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: maximize pumping subject to the torque limits and one control-Lyapunov constraint. The constraint uses the model-based rate of the error, so no stabilizing feedback gain is needed. Experiments in hardware show swing-ups along both modes and compare the allocation with summing-and-clipping and with prioritized stabilization.

## New “HAMR-E” robots could enable inspection of complex machines without dismantling them

By Lindsay Brownell

(CAMBRIDGE, Mass) — Jet engines can have up to 25,000 individual parts, making regular maintenance a tedious task that can take over a month per engine. Many components are located deep inside the engine and cannot be inspected without taking the machine apart, adding time and costs to maintenance. # Cross- link collective: Entangled robotic matter with cohesive motion 

Danna Ma 1, Baxi Chong 2, Daniel I. Goldman 3, Kirstin H. Petersen 1*

Robotic applications increasingly demand systems that are resilient, adaptable, and scalable. One promising route is through collectives of simple modules, where complex group-level behavior emerges from local interactions. By omitting fixed topologies and tight coordination, this approach sacrifices predictability and conventional tools for behaviors inherently optimized through stochastic mechanical interactions. A key challenge is maintaining cohe-sion and functionality without fixed connections and explicit coordination. We introduce the cross-link collective, a physically entangled robotic system inspired by cross-linking in active gels. Through shape morphing and transient entanglement, individually immobile modules produce sustained collective motion. The mechanically intelligent robot matter favors chains and phase relationships that reduce joint torques and reconfigures in response to per-turbations. We show that distributed control can be added to this substrate to further enhance cohesion. Leverag-ing weak, reversible connections, the cross-link collective is adaptable, scalable, and fault tolerant, offering insights to applications from soft matter and robotics.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9944140/)Abstract

Climbing robots are designed to conduct tasks that may be dangerous for humans working at height. In addition to improving safety, they can also increase task efficiency and reduce labor costs. They are widely used for bridge inspection, high-rise building cleaning, fruit picking, high-altitude rescue, and military reconnaissance. In addition to climbing, these robots need to carry tools to complete their tasks. Hence, their design and development are more challenging than those of most other robots. This paper analyzes and compares the past decade’s design and development of climbing robots that can ascend vertical structures such as rods, cables, walls, and trees. Firstly, the main research fields and basic design requirements of climbing robots are introduced, and then the advantages and disadvantages of six key technologies are summarized, namely, conceptual design, adhesion methods, locomotion modes, safety mechanisms, control methods, and operational tools. Finally, the remaining challenges in research on climbing robots are briefly discussed and future research directions are highlighted. This paper provides a scientific reference for researchers engaged in the study of climbing robots.

**Keywords:**vertical structure, climbing robot, application fields, adhesion mechanism, locomotion mode, control mode, operation tools

jina.title: This Robot Doesn’t Need Any Electronics
jina.snippet:
[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X5caSAb4kz0)

Engineers at the University of California San Diego have created a four-legged soft robot that doesn't need any electronics to work. The robot only needs a constant source of pressurized air for all its functions, including its controls and locomotion systems.

The team, led by Michael T. Tolley, a professor of mechanical engineering at the Jacobs School of Engineering at UC San Diego, details its findings in the Feb. 17, 2021 issue of the journal Science Robotics.

"This work represents a fundamental yet significant step towards fully-autonomous, electronics-free walking robots,"said Dylan Drotman, a Ph.D. student in Tolley's research group and the paper's first author.

Applications include low-cost robotics for entertainment, such as toys, and robots that can operate in environments where electronics cannot function, such as MRI machines or mine shafts. Soft robots are of particular interest because they easily adapt to their environment and operate safely near humans.

Most soft robots are powered by pressurized air and are controlled by electronic circuits. But this approach requires complex components like circuit boards, valves and pumps--often outside the robot's body. These components, which constitute the robot's brains and nervous system, are typically bulky and expensive. By contrast, the UC San Diego robot is controlled by a light-weight, low-cost system of pneumatic circuits, made up of tubes and soft valves, onboard the robot itself. The robot can walk on command or in response to signals it senses from the environment.

"With our approach, you could make a very complex robotic brain,"said Tolley, the study's senior author. "Our focus here was to make the simplest air-powered nervous system needed to control walking."

keenable.title: Natural Swing-Up of an Underpowered Double Pendulum
keenable.snippet:
Swinging up a robot whose motors cannot even hold its arm horizontal is a matter of timing, not of force. The direct-drive motors of the planar two-link robot of Fig. 1 deliver only 1.1 Nm, about 6 % of the gravity torque in the first joint with the arm held horizontally. With full torque in both joints, link 2 tilts by 16.3^∘ and link 1 stays hanging, because the reaction of the elbow torque cancels the shoulder torque (Fig. 1b). Neither a joint PD controller nor a controller that tracks a direct path to the upright pose (Fig. 5a) can get there; the robot has to collect the energy over many swings. A single pendulum is swung up by energy control, which puts it on the homoclinic orbit that ends upright [1]. The double pendulum is chaotic [2], so energy control alone most likely ends in chaotic motion, and energy-based swing-ups of double pendulums pass through intermediate equilibria [3, 4]. We instead guide the swing-up along the NNMs of the robot [5, 6, 7], families of periodic orbits of the free dynamics, one per energy. On one mode the robot behaves much like a single pendulum: there is no chaos, and the modes connect the hanging equilibrium to a homoclinic orbit at the upright one [8]. Pumping energy along a mode thus carries the robot from rest to almost upright, where a short precomputed trajectory catches it in a handstand.

keenable.title: A robot arm with very weak motors swings itself upright by riding its natural motion
keenable.snippet:
Researchers led by [Arne Sachtler](https://dronenews.org/entity/arne-sachtler) have made a two-link robot arm swing itself up although its direct-drive motors deliver only about 6% of the torque that gravity puts on its shoulder, according to a paper on arXiv. Instead of fighting the arm's dynamics, the controller follows its nonlinear normal modes, families of periodic swinging motions.
Adding energy pushes the arm away from those motions, so pumping energy in and keeping the arm on its path compete for the same small torque. The team splits the motor torque into a steering part that adds no energy and a pumping part, and at each moment solves a small linear program that pumps as hard as the torque limits allow while a stability condition holds, without a feedback gain to tune.
In hardware experiments the arm swung up along both of its modes, and the researchers compared the method with two simpler ways of combining the motor commands.

keenable.title: Swing-Up of a Weakly Actuated Double Pendulum via Nonlinear Normal Modes
keenable.snippet: We identify the nonlinear normal modes spawning from the stable equilibrium of a double pendulum under gravity, and we establish their connection to homoclinic orbits through the unstable upright position as energy increases. This result is exploited to devise an efficient swing-up strategy for a double pendulum with weak, saturating actuators. Our approach involves stabilizing the system onto periodic orbits associated with the nonlinear modes while gradually injecting energy. Since these modes are autonomous system evolutions, the required control effort for stabilization is minimal. Even with actuator limitations of less than 1% of the maximum gravitational torque, the proposed method accomplishes the swing-up of the double pendulum by allowing sufficient time.

keenable.title: Energy based control of the Pendubot
keenable.snippet:
The two-link underactuated robotic mechanism called the Pendubot is used for research in nonlinear control and for education in various concepts like nonlinear dynamics, robotics and control system design.
This device is a two-link planar robot with an actuator at the shoulder (link 1) and no actuator at the elbow (link 2). The link 2 moves freely around link 1 and the control objective is to bring the mechanism to the unstable equilibrium points.

The controller that we propose is not based on the standard techniques of feedback linearization (or partial feedback linearization). We believe that our approach is the first for which a complete stability analysis has been presented.
The stabilization algorithm proposed here is an adaptation of the work of [8] which deals with the inverted pendulum. We will consider the passivity properties of the pendubot and use an energy based approach to establish the proposed control law. The control algorithm as well as the convergence analysis are based on Lyapunov theory.

We have presented a control strategy for the pendubot that brings the state either arbitrarily close to the top position or to a homoclinic orbit that will eventually enter the basin of attraction of any locally convergent controller. The control strategy is based on an energy approach and the passivity properties of the pendubot. A Lyapunov function is obtained using the total energy of the system. The analysis is carried out using the LaSalle's theorem.

keenable.snippet: Acrobot For example with an acrobot, which is a two-link pendulum, whose first link is not actuated whereas the second one is actuated, authors of [6] and [18] define a method in two stages. At first, a slow swinging up process, founded on a passivity-based approach, brings the acrobot close to the upright position. After switching control to a balancing linear controller, the pendulum is locally asymptotically stabilized around its upright equilibrium position. A new control law to swing up an acrobot and to stabilize it in the upright position is developed in [19]. A swing-up controller that can bring a n-link revolute acrobot is considered by Xin et al. [20]. The first joint of the acrobot is passive and the others are actuated. The swing-up controller can bring the robot into any arbitrarily small neighborhood of the upright equilibrium point with all links in the upright position. The strategy is first to iteratively devise a series of virtual composite links to be used for designing a coordinate transformation on the angles of all the active joints. Second, an energy-based swing-up controller that uses a new Lyapunov function based on that transformation is devised. Conditions on the control parameters are established to ensure attainment of the swing-up control objective.

keenable.title: EigenMPC: An Eigenmanifold-Inspired Model-Predictive Control Framework for Exciting Efficient Oscillations in Mechanical Systems
keenable.snippet: This paper proposes a Nonlinear Model-Predictive Control (NMPC) method capable of finding and converging to energy-efficient regular oscillations, which require no control action to be sustained. The approach builds up on the recently developed Eigenmanifold theory, which defines the sets of line-shaped oscillations of a robot as an invariant two-dimensional submanifold of its state space. By defining the control problem as a nonlinear program (NLP), the controller is able to deal with constraints in the state and control variables and be energy-efficient not only in its final trajectory but also during the convergence phase. An initial implementation of this approach is proposed, analyzed, and tested in simulation.

keenable.title: Explosive Legged Robotic Hopping: Energy Accumulation and Power Amplification via Pneumatic Augmentation
keenable.snippet:
We present a novel pneumatic augmentation to traditional electric motor-actuated legged robot to increase intermittent power density to perform infrequent explosive hopping behaviors. The pneumatic system is composed of a pneumatic pump, a tank, and a pneumatic actuator. The tank is charged up by the pump during regular hopping motion that is created by the electric motors. At any time after reaching a desired air pressure in the tank, a solenoid valve is utilized to rapidly release the air pressure to the pneumatic actuator (piston) which is used in conjunction with the electric motors to perform explosive hopping, increasing maximum hopping height for one or subsequent cycles. We show that, on a custom-designed one-legged hopping robot, without any additional power source and with this novel pneumatic augmentation system, their associated system identification and optimal control, the robot is able to realize highly explosive hopping with power amplification per cycle by a factor of approximately 5.4 times the power of electric motor actuation alone.

To address this problem, we propose a design and control framework that augments legged robots with a pneumatic system to accumulate energy during the periods of negative work for storage over multiple cycles. With this system, a pump converts this kinetic energy to potential energy in the form of compressed air pumped to a tank. As an integrated part of the system, no special pumping phase is necessary, as the pump performs its energy conversion during normal locomotion activities. Each cycle pumps additional air, increasing the potential energy in the tank. When the tank has reached a desired pressure (sufficient potential energy), the air can be released, rapidly displacing a pneumatic actuator (converted back to kinetic energy) which is utilized in conjunction with the original actuator to amplify power output for explosive locomotion behaviors.

keenable.title: Swing-up control for a two-link underactuated robot with a flexible elbow joint: New results beyond the passive elbow joint
keenable.snippet:
This paper concerns the swing-up control problem for a two-link underactuated planar robot moving in the vertical plane with a single actuator at the base joint and a spring between the two links. This indicates that the robot has an active base joint and a flexible elbow joint; and below we call it the AF robot,

This paper presents two new properties of the AF robot in the presence of gravity. One property is about its linear controllability (the controllability of the linearized model of a nonlinear system around an equilibrium point [12]). We obtain a necessary and sufficient condition on the mechanical parameters of the robot and the spring constant such that the robot is linearly controllable at the UEP. We reveal that the linear controllability at the UEP is destroyed when the spring constant takes a value determined by the mechanical parameters of the two-links. This is a surprising result since the two extreme cases of the AF robot, the Pendubot and a one-link rigid robot (with the spring constant being 0 and ∞, respectively), are always linearly controllable at the UEP without any condition on their mechanical parameters. Another property is about the limitation of the PD control.

We present a novel pneumatic augmentation to traditional electric motor-actuated legged robot to increase intermittent power density to perform infrequent explosive hopping behaviors. The pneumatic system is composed of a pneumatic pump, a tank, and a pneumatic actuator. The tank is charged up by the pump during regular hopping motion that is created by the electric motors. At any time after reaching a desired air pressure in the tank, a solenoid valve is utilized to rapidly release the air pressure to the pneumatic actuator (piston) which is used in conjunction with the electric motors to perform explosive hopping, increasing maximum hopping height for one or subsequent cycles. We show that, on a custom-designed one-legged hopping robot, without any additional power source and with this novel pneumatic augmentation system, their associated system identification and optimal control, the robot is able to realize highly explosive hopping with power amplification per cycle by a factor of approximately 5.4 times the power of electric motor actuation alone.

To address this problem, we propose a design and control framework that augments legged robots with a pneumatic system to accumulate energy during the periods of negative work for storage over multiple cycles. With this system, a pump converts this kinetic energy to potential energy in the form of compressed air pumped to a tank. As an integrated part of the system, no special pumping phase is necessary, as the pump performs its energy conversion during normal locomotion activities. Each cycle pumps additional air, increasing the potential energy in the tank. When the tank has reached a desired pressure (sufficient potential energy), the air can be released, rapidly displacing a pneumatic actuator (converted back to kinetic energy) which is utilized in conjunction with the original actuator to amplify power output for explosive locomotion behaviors.

octen.title: FlipWalker: Jacob's Ladder toy-inspired robot for locomotion across diverse, complex terrain
octen.snippet: This paper introduces FlipWalker, a novel underactuated robot locomotion system inspired by Jacob's Ladder illusion toy, designed to traverse challenging terrains where wheeled robots often struggle. Like the Jacob's Ladder toy, FlipWalker features two interconnected segments joined by flexible cables, enabling it to pivot and flip around singularities in a manner reminiscent of the toy's cascading motion. Actuation is provided by motor-driven legs within each segment that push off either the ground or the opposing segment, depending on the robot's current configuration. A physics-based model of the underactuated flipping dynamics is formulated to elucidate the critical design parameters governing forward motion and obstacle clearance or climbing. The untethered prototype weighs 0.78 kg, achieves a maximum flipping speed of 0.2 body lengths per second. Arne Sachtler ² _,_ ¹ , Manuel Keppler ¹ _,_ ³ , Florian Loeffl ¹ , and Alin Albu-Sch¨affer ¹ _,_ ²

**_Abstract_** **—Robots with weak motors must ride their natural dynamics rather than fight them. We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6 % of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits. On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque. Investigates the problem of swing up control of the Acrobot, a two-link, underactuated robot that is a useful vehicle to study problems in nonlinear control. # A robot arm with very weak motors swings itself upright by riding its natural motion

Its motors deliver only about 6% of the torque gravity puts on its shoulder, so the controller pumps energy along the arm's natural swinging motions.

12 November 2026

Share ＋ Save story

A computer drawing of the two-link robot arm with its motors. ⤢ Image: Arne Sachtler et al. via arXiv

Researchers led by [Arne Sachtler](dronenews.org/entity/arne-sachtler) have made a two-link robot arm swing itself up although its direct-drive motors deliver only about 6% of the torque that gravity puts on its shoulder, according to a paper on arXiv. Instead of fighting the arm's dynamics, the controller follows its nonlinear normal modes, families of periodic swinging motions.

Adding energy pushes the arm away from those motions, so pumping energy in and keeping the arm on its path compete for the same small torque. The team splits the motor torque into a steering part that adds no energy and a pumping part, and at each moment solves a small linear program that pumps as hard as the torque limits allow while a stability condition holds, without a feedback gain to tune.

In hardware experiments the arm swung up along both of its modes, and the researchers compared the method with two simpler ways of combining the motor commands.

[Source: arXiv Robotics (cs.RO)](arxiv.org/abs/2611.17575)

## The system

The acrobot is a two-link, serial-chain planar pendulum. The system has **two degrees of freedom** ( $q\_1$ and $q\_2$ ) but only **one actuator** ( $u\_2$ ) acting on the elbow joint. William R. Provancher ∗ , Member, IEEE, Samuel I. Jensen-Segal, and Mark A. Fehlberg
Abstract —We present a novel bioinspired dynamic climbing
robot, with a recursive name: ROCR is an Oscillating Climbing Robot. ROCR, pronounced “Rocker,” is a pendular, two-link, serial-chain robot that utilizes alternating hand-holds and an actuated tail to propel itself upward in a climbing style based on observation of human climbers and brachiating gibbons. ROCR’s bioinspired pendular climbing strategy is simple and efficient. In fact, to our knowledge ROCR is also the first climbing robot that is designed for efficiency. ROCR is a lightweight, flexible, self-contained robot. This robot is intended for autonomous surveillance and inspection on sheer vertical surfaces. Potential locomotion gait strategies were investigated in simulation using Working Model 2D, and were evaluated on a basis of climbing rate, energy efficiency, and whether stable open-loop climbing was achieved. We identified that the most effective climbing resulted from sinusoidal tail motions. The addition of a body stabilizer reduced the robot’s out-of-plane motion at higher frequencies and promoted more reliable gripper attachment. Experimental measurements of the robot showed climbing ef- ficiencies of over 20% and a specific resistance of 5.0, while consuming 27 J/m at a maximum climbing speed of 15.7 cm/s (0.34 body lengths/s) – setting a first benchmark for efficiency of climbing robots. Future work will include further design optimization, integration of more complex gripping mechanisms, and investigating more complex control strategies.

Abstract

This paper concerns the swing-up control of an underactuated two-link robot with a linear torsional spring-attached ﬁrst joint and an actuated second joint (called the FA robot below) moving in a vertical plane. First, we present a necessary and sufficient condition such the FA robot is linearly controllable at the upright equilibrium point (UEP, where two links are both upright). For the case that the total mechanical energy of the FA robot converges to its desired value, we present its phase portrait. For the case that the convergence is not achieved, we show that the FA robot approaches an equilibrium point belonging to a set of equilibrium points, and propose a sufficient condition to check its stability. # Title: Natural Swing-Up of an Underpowered Double Pendulum
Authors:Arne Sachtler, Manuel Keppler, Florian Loeffl, Alin Albu-Schäffer View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract:Robots with weak motors must ride their natural dynamics rather than fight them.
We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6\,\% of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits.
On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque.
We split the input torque into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy.
The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: maximize pumping subject to the torque limits and one control-Lyapunov constraint.
The constraint uses the model-based rate of the error, so no stabilizing feedback gain is needed.
Experiments in hardware show swing-ups along both modes and compare the allocation with summing-and-clipping and with prioritized stabilization.

seltz.title: The Double Pendulum — Classical Mechanics
seltz.snippet:
The driven damped pendulum of the previous article needed three ingredients for chaos — nonlinearity, dissipation, forcing — and a hidden third dimension smuggled in through the drive phase. The double pendulum needs none of that apparatus. Hang one pendulum from the bob of another, lift the pair to horizontal, let go. No motor, no friction worth modelling, energy exactly conserved, equations derivable in ten lines of Lagrangian mechanics — and the motion is so sensitive to its starting point that no computer on Earth can forecast the third flip of the lower arm from any realistic measurement of the release. This article is the course's cleanest specimen of *Hamiltonian* chaos, and it earns that role by an exact count. Two rods give two degrees of freedom: a four-dimensional phase space (θ1,θ2,p1,p2)(\theta_1, \theta_2, p_1, p_2). Time-independence gives one conserved quantity: the energy. The Liouville–Arnold theorem of the W4 articles says integrability — motion forever on invariant tori — requires as many independent commuting constants as degrees of freedom: two. The double pendulum has one. That missing second integral is not a technical footnote; it is the entire story. Trajectories are confined to a three-dimensional energy surface but not to two-dimensional tori within it, and in the room left over, chaos lives. The system is also the perfect stage for the KAM theorem in action. At low energy the coupling barely flexes and quasiperiodic tori dominate — the Poincaré section shows nested closed curves, a portrait of near-integrability. Feed in more energy and resonant tori shred into island chains, chaotic layers widen around broken separatrices, and above the energy at which the inner arm can flip over the top, a connected chaotic sea floods most of the surface. One tabletop toy walks you from Liouville's ordered world to Poincaré's tangled one, with the crossover controlled by a single dial: energy.

Stand a broomstick on your open palm and you already know the algorithm. The moment the stick tips, you slide your hand toward the lean — putting the support back under the falling top. seltz.title: Physical reservoir learns to swing up a pendulum without a model
seltz.snippet:
A pendulum that swings itself upright using nothing more than the chaotic motion of two double pendulums as its brain sounds like a curiosity from a robotics lab, and that is exactly what it is. Researchers at the University of Cambridge and Kyushu University have introduced a scheme they call physical reservoir control, in which a purely mechanical system learns to act as the controller of a separate machine. Instead of writing down equations for the plant being controlled, the team let a physical object absorb data, compute with its own dynamics, and emit the signals that keep a torque-limited pendulum balanced. The work, published in Communications Engineering, demonstrates swing-up and upright balancing in both simulation and a real-world setup, and shows that the learned coupling can survive noise, impulses, and even brief sensor blackouts.

The idea builds on reservoir computing, a machine-learning framework in which a fixed nonlinear dynamical system projects inputs into a high-dimensional space and only a simple linear readout is trained. Earlier reservoir-control studies used recurrent neural networks as the reservoir, which demands substantial computation and sits far from the way biology seems to work. The new study replaces the network with hardware: a pair of double pendulums whose first joints are driven by servo motors and whose second joints swing freely. Optical markers on every joint let cameras reconstruct the reservoir state in real time. The plant is a single pendulum simulated in MATLAB Simulink that exchanges signals bidirectionally with the physical reservoir, so the coupling is partly embodied and partly electronic.

seltz.title: Humanoid Balance Control: A Robot Crossed the Monkey Bars | HiWave Blog
seltz.snippet:
On September 11, 2026, IEEE Spectrum’s weekly robot video roundup led with a humanoid robot jumping up onto a set of monkey bars and swinging across. It looks like a stunt. It isn’t. Humanoid balance control on a flat floor is a solved-ish problem that dozens of companies now ship; balance control while hanging from two thin steel bars, with your feet off the ground and your whole body swinging, is a different mathematical problem with a different failure mode. The gap between those two things explains most of what’s confusing about robot videos right now.

## Key Takeaways

- The robot came from ETH Zurich’s Robotic Systems Lab, and the published framing of the work is specific: “Traversing sparse 3D structures requires humanoid robots to perceive thin, overhanging geometry while executing agile, accurate whole-body motions.”
- Walking balance keeps the robot’s center of mass over a *support polygon* on the ground. Hanging balance has no support polygon: the robot manages angular momentum around a grip point instead.
- The perception half is as hard as the control half. Most legged robots build a 2.5D height map of the floor. A monkey bar is thin, has nothing under it, and breaks that representation.
- This is a research demo, not a product. Evan Ackerman’s September 2025 IEEE Spectrum analysis found that even the leading humanoid companies had deployed “only a small handful of robots in carefully controlled pilot projects.”
- For a kid, the useful lesson is the one engineers actually use: balance is not a feeling, it’s a prediction. The robot is constantly guessing where its body will be a quarter-second from now.

ultimate.title: Natural Swing-Up of an Underpowered Double Pendulum
ultimate.snippet:
Swinging up a robot whose motors cannot even hold its arm horizontal is a matter of timing, not of force. The direct-drive motors of the planar two-link robot of Fig. 1 deliver only 1.1 Nm, about 6 % of the gravity torque in the first joint with the arm held horizontally. With full torque in both joints, link 2 tilts by 16.3^∘ and link 1 stays hanging, because the reaction of the elbow torque cancels the shoulder torque (Fig. 1b). Neither a joint PD controller nor a controller that tracks a direct path to the upright pose (Fig. 5a) can get there; the robot has to collect the energy over many swings. A single pendulum is swung up by energy control, which puts it on the homoclinic orbit that ends upright [1]. The double pendulum is chaotic [2], so energy control alone most likely ends in chaotic motion, and energy-based swing-ups of double pendulums pass through intermediate equilibria [3, 4]. We instead guide the swing-up along the NNMs of the robot [5, 6, 7], families of periodic orbits of the free dynamics, one per energy. On one mode the robot behaves much like a single pendulum: there is no chaos, and the modes connect the hanging equilibrium to a homoclinic orbit at the upright one [8]. Pumping energy along a mode thus carries the robot from rest to almost upright, where a short precomputed trajectory catches it in a handstand.

ultimate.title: A robot arm with very weak motors swings itself upright by riding its natural motion
ultimate.snippet:
Researchers led by [Arne Sachtler](https://dronenews.org/entity/arne-sachtler) have made a two-link robot arm swing itself up although its direct-drive motors deliver only about 6% of the torque that gravity puts on its shoulder, according to a paper on arXiv. Instead of fighting the arm's dynamics, the controller follows its nonlinear normal modes, families of periodic swinging motions.
Adding energy pushes the arm away from those motions, so pumping energy in and keeping the arm on its path compete for the same small torque. The team splits the motor torque into a steering part that adds no energy and a pumping part, and at each moment solves a small linear program that pumps as hard as the torque limits allow while a stability condition holds, without a feedback gain to tune.
In hardware experiments the arm swung up along both of its modes, and the researchers compared the method with two simpler ways of combining the motor commands.

ultimate.title: Swing-Up of a Weakly Actuated Double Pendulum via Nonlinear Normal Modes
ultimate.snippet: We identify the nonlinear normal modes spawning from the stable equilibrium of a double pendulum under gravity, and we establish their connection to homoclinic orbits through the unstable upright position as energy increases. This result is exploited to devise an efficient swing-up strategy for a double pendulum with weak, saturating actuators. Our approach involves stabilizing the system onto periodic orbits associated with the nonlinear modes while gradually injecting energy. Since these modes are autonomous system evolutions, the required control effort for stabilization is minimal. Even with actuator limitations of less than 1% of the maximum gravitational torque, the proposed method accomplishes the swing-up of the double pendulum by allowing sufficient time.

ultimate.title: Energy based control of the Pendubot
ultimate.snippet:
The two-link underactuated robotic mechanism called the Pendubot is used for research in nonlinear control and for education in various concepts like nonlinear dynamics, robotics and control system design.
This device is a two-link planar robot with an actuator at the shoulder (link 1) and no actuator at the elbow (link 2). The link 2 moves freely around link 1 and the control objective is to bring the mechanism to the unstable equilibrium points.

The controller that we propose is not based on the standard techniques of feedback linearization (or partial feedback linearization). We believe that our approach is the first for which a complete stability analysis has been presented.
The stabilization algorithm proposed here is an adaptation of the work of [8] which deals with the inverted pendulum. We will consider the passivity properties of the pendubot and use an energy based approach to establish the proposed control law. The control algorithm as well as the convergence analysis are based on Lyapunov theory.

We have presented a control strategy for the pendubot that brings the state either arbitrarily close to the top position or to a homoclinic orbit that will eventually enter the basin of attraction of any locally convergent controller. The control strategy is based on an energy approach and the passivity properties of the pendubot. A Lyapunov function is obtained using the total energy of the system. The analysis is carried out using the LaSalle's theorem.

ultimate.title: Energy-based Swing-up Control for a Two-link Underactuated Robot with Flexible First Joint
ultimate.snippet: This paper concerns the swing-up control of an underactuated two-link robot with a linear torsional spring-attached ﬁrst joint and an actuated second joint (called the FA robot below) moving in a vertical plane. First, we present a necessary and sufficient condition such the FA robot is linearly controllable at the upright equilibrium point (UEP, where two links are both upright). Second, we prove without any assumption that the FA robot is at an equilibrium point provided that its actuated joint angle is constant under a constant torque. Third, for the FA robot with its torsional stiﬀness of the spring being smaller than a value determined by the coefficients of its gravitational terms, we propose an energy-based controller without singular points to swing it up. We conduct a global motion analysis for the FA robot under the proposed controller. For the case that the total mechanical energy of the FA robot converges to its desired value, we present its phase portrait. For the case that the convergence is not achieved, we show that the FA robot approaches an equilibrium point belonging to a set of equilibrium points, and propose a sufficient condition to check its stability. From the motion analysis, we present a sufficient condition such that the FA robot can be swung-up close to the UEP under the proposed swing-up controller. Finally, we verify our theoretical results through a numerical simulation.

ultimate.title: EigenMPC: An Eigenmanifold-Inspired Model-Predictive Control Framework for Exciting Efficient Oscillations in Mechanical Systems
ultimate.snippet: This paper proposes a Nonlinear Model-Predictive Control (NMPC) method capable of finding and converging to energy-efficient regular oscillations, which require no control action to be sustained. The approach builds up on the recently developed Eigenmanifold theory, which defines the sets of line-shaped oscillations of a robot as an invariant two-dimensional submanifold of its state space. By defining the control problem as a nonlinear program (NLP), the controller is able to deal with constraints in the state and control variables and be energy-efficient not only in its final trajectory but also during the convergence phase. An initial implementation of this approach is proposed, analyzed, and tested in simulation.

ultimate.title: Explosive Legged Robotic Hopping: Energy Accumulation and Power Amplification via Pneumatic Augmentation
ultimate.snippet:
We present a novel pneumatic augmentation to traditional electric motor-actuated legged robot to increase intermittent power density to perform infrequent explosive hopping behaviors. The pneumatic system is composed of a pneumatic pump, a tank, and a pneumatic actuator. The tank is charged up by the pump during regular hopping motion that is created by the electric motors. At any time after reaching a desired air pressure in the tank, a solenoid valve is utilized to rapidly release the air pressure to the pneumatic actuator (piston) which is used in conjunction with the electric motors to perform explosive hopping, increasing maximum hopping height for one or subsequent cycles. We show that, on a custom-designed one-legged hopping robot, without any additional power source and with this novel pneumatic augmentation system, their associated system identification and optimal control, the robot is able to realize highly explosive hopping with power amplification per cycle by a factor of approximately 5.4 times the power of electric motor actuation alone.

To address this problem, we propose a design and control framework that augments legged robots with a pneumatic system to accumulate energy during the periods of negative work for storage over multiple cycles. With this system, a pump converts this kinetic energy to potential energy in the form of compressed air pumped to a tank. As an integrated part of the system, no special pumping phase is necessary, as the pump performs its energy conversion during normal locomotion activities. Each cycle pumps additional air, increasing the potential energy in the tank. When the tank has reached a desired pressure (sufficient potential energy), the air can be released, rapidly displacing a pneumatic actuator (converted back to kinetic energy) which is utilized in conjunction with the original actuator to amplify power output for explosive locomotion behaviors.
